done.why: I played about 276 turns and got through the house, the dam and reservoir, the temple and Egyptian room, and the canyon and rainbow, with 164 of 350 points. The lamp was getting dim. There was more left (the river by boat, the maze, the trident, the thief's lair), but I had read a lot of the writing and the rest felt like a long haul of carrying things back and forth. I stopped at a good resting point, with nine treasures in the case.

about: A white house in the woods, and an empire of tunnels under it, both emptied out long ago. You loot what the empire's tyrants, gods and artists left behind and carry it up to a trophy case that waits patiently to be filled. A lot of the writing is about objects that have outlived the people and purposes they were made for: a coffin face that doesn't know its king is gone, weed in a drained room hanging in "disappointed" strands, a bubble "waiting to be told it may begin".

moments.note: First examine that went beyond the stock text. The boarded door was nailed by 'someone in more of a hurry than a carpenter'. That told me the descriptions would reward looking closely.
The troll's description: teeth 'not all of them his own', and he swings the axe 'the way other people tap a foot'. Funny and menacing at once.

I died to the troll, and the resurrection text was new and charming. Plain things were strewn about the fields, valuables had rolled into dark corners, and 'somebody tidy has put the lamp back'. I liked collecting my things afterwards.
The chasm as 'a black slot in the floor of the world', with cold air 'smelling of nothing at all'.
The green bubble's description changed after I pushed the yellow button: from 'waiting to be told it may begin' to 'ready when you are'. A puzzle clue told through the writing. Lovely.
'Your load is too heavy, the sword not least of it.' Even the refusal had a voice, and it told me what to drop.
The platinum bar is 'quite silent, which in this room is a distinction'. A joke that ties the object to the Loud Room it was lying in.
The chimney refusal listed exactly what I carried and the rule: 'you, your lamp and one thing more, and not an inch besides.' Clear and well phrased.
I took the ivory torch and the thief robbed me of everything except the lamp, in one move. I had left the sword in the Loud Room, so that was my own fault. Still, it stung.
The coffin face is 'very sure of its place in the world' and doesn't seem to know Ramses has been moved. My favourite line.
On top of a rainbow, 'look down' gave 'You see the floor, where you left it.' That's a stock joke, and it didn't fit a rainbow over a 450-foot waterfall.
The pot of gold is 'exactly where the stories say it would be, which is somehow the most surprising thing about it.'
Every trip down the trap door it crashed shut and was barred again. Going back and forth by chimney with one item at a time got tedious.

wished: I wished I could look out from the rainbow and get a description of the falls and canyon from up there, not the stock floor joke.
I wished I could ask the thief for my torch back or bargain with him. He 'does not speak', and he left before I could try anything.
I wished the trap door stayed open once I had found another way out, so I didn't have to make so many single-item trips through the chimney.
I wished the Round Room listed its open exits. I had to guess directions.

lines.line: boarded across with planks nailed every which way, by someone in more of a hurry than a carpenter. Whatever the owners meant by it, they did not mean visitors.
lines.why: This set the tone: dry, observant, and it gives the house a history.

lines.line: He is watching you the way a cook watches a chicken.
lines.why: Funny and frightening in one image.

lines.line: anything of value has rolled into some dark corner in or under it, and somebody tidy has put the lamp back in the living room.
lines.why: It made dying feel like part of the world, and the world a little cosy.

lines.line: a black slot in the floor of the world, too deep for any light to find the bottom. A cold air comes up out of it, smelling of nothing at all.
lines.why: The best piece of atmosphere I read.

lines.line: It is glowing serenely, the calm, untroubled green of a machine that is ready when you are.
lines.why: The description changes with the world's state. It works as prose and as a clue.

lines.line: weed hangs from the carvings in long, dry, disappointed strands.
lines.why: One adjective, 'disappointed', makes a whole drained civilization sad.

lines.line: It is cold to the touch, and quite silent, which in this room is a distinction.
lines.why: A joke that comes from where the bar was found.

lines.line: Ramses II was buried in it, and has evidently been moved elsewhere since, which the face does not seem to know.
lines.why: Melancholy and comic at once. My favourite line in the game.

lines.line: It is exactly where the stories say it would be, which is somehow the most surprising thing about it.
lines.why: A nice turn on the oldest cliché there is.

fun.why: Killing the troll on the second try, draining the reservoir to uncover the trunk, praying my way out of the temple, and walking the rainbow were all satisfying. The thief stripping me at the torch, and the repeated trips through the trap door and chimney, wore on me.

engagement.why: The added descriptions kept me examining everything. I examined almost every object because the writing kept rewarding it. Engagement dropped in the long ferrying stretches between the cellar and the case.

difficulty.why: The puzzles were fair, and the text pointed at them: the bubble changing, the chimney stating its rule, 'the sword not least of it' telling me what to drop. The troll and the thief add real danger without being cruel.

interestingness.why: The familiar structure is there, but the new examine text gives objects a past and a mood, like the coffin face, the pedestal 'made for one thing to stand on it', and the rope coiled 'with more care than anything else'. The new death text and the rule-stating refusals made the world feel looked after.

prose.why: Most of the new prose is excellent: precise, wry, and economical, with one exact word doing the work ('disappointed', 'distinction', 'tidy'). It also sits comfortably alongside the original text. The one jarring moment was the stock 'floor, where you left it' answer on the rainbow, and a few rooms just repeat their names on return. Neither spoils it.
